title: Choose a learning signal and trace data preparation, train-validation-test separation, training, serving, and monitoring without confusing a model with the whole ML system

questions.prompt:
A bicycle-hire service predicts each station’s number of rentals during the next hour. Historical records contain weather forecasts, rentals before prediction time, actual next-hour rentals, and some missing weather values.

Explain which learning signal fits this task, how the inputs should be prepared, and what training learns.

rubric.point: Explains that supervised learning fits because recorded next-hour rental counts provide known targets.
Explains that features must be available at prediction time; actual next-hour rentals belong only in the target because using them as inputs leaks the answer.
Explains that missing weather values need a defined, deterministic treatment so records become usable model inputs.
Explains that training fits a mapping from inputs to rental counts by reducing prediction error against training targets.

questions.model: This is supervised regression: each historical example has a known target, the next hour’s rental count. Inputs can include forecasts available at prediction time and earlier rentals. Actual rentals during the predicted hour must remain the target; using them as features would reveal the answer. Missing weather values need a deterministic rule, such as a defined replacement plus a missing-value indicator. Training fits an input-to-count mapping by reducing error between predictions and the training targets.

questions.prompt:
The bicycle-hire service has two years of hourly records and will forecast future hours. An engineer randomly mixes all hours, then repeatedly chooses model settings using the reported test score.

Explain why this evaluation can mislead, and explain the distinct roles of training, validation, and test data in a better evaluation.

rubric.point: Explains that chronological separation better represents forecasting future hours; random mixing can let later conditions inform evaluation of earlier periods.
Explains that training data is used to fit the model.
Explains that validation data guides model or hyperparameter choices.
Explains that a later test holdout estimates performance after choices are fixed; repeatedly choosing settings from its score turns it into validation data.

questions.model: Use earlier records for training, a later period for validation, and a still later period for testing. This better matches the real task: learning from the past to predict the future. Random mixing can hide changes over time by allowing later conditions into training. Training fits the model; validation guides choices such as model settings. The test holdout estimates performance after those choices are fixed. Repeatedly choosing settings from test results makes that set part of tuning, so its score no longer provides an independent final check.

questions.prompt:
The rental model is deployed to produce forecasts every hour. Forecast jobs finish successfully, but weather inputs have shifted. Actual rental counts arrive the following day.

Explain why deploying the trained model alone does not complete the ML system, what monitoring can establish immediately versus later, and whether the input shift alone justifies retraining.

rubric.point: Explains that serving also requires timely feature collection and the same preprocessing used during training.
Distinguishes immediate service and input checks, such as forecast completion, latency, errors, missing values, or drift, from predictive-quality measurements.
Explains that predictive quality is measured by comparing forecasts with actual rental counts once those targets arrive.
Explains that drift alone does not prove worse predictions; retraining needs a measurable trigger and the resulting model must pass evaluation before promotion.

questions.model: The model is one component. Hourly serving must collect available features and apply the same preprocessing used in training before producing forecasts. Job completion, latency, errors, missing inputs, and input drift can be checked immediately. Successful execution does not establish accurate predictions. The next day, forecasts can be compared with actual rental counts to measure prediction error. Changed weather inputs are a warning, not proof of degraded quality. Retraining should follow a defined, measurable trigger, and a replacement model must pass evaluation before promotion.
